verdict.rationale: The wording across 2 Corinthians 2, Galatians 6, James 5, Luke 17, and the Leviticus 19 root all points the same way: forgiveness, mending, and reaffirmed love toward the repentant offender. In 2 Corinthians 2:6-8 the corporate censure (epitimia) imposed 'by the majority' (hypo ton pleionon) is called 'sufficient' (ikanon), and the assembly is told to 'forgive, graciously grant' (charisasthai, a completed past action in infinitive form) and 'comfort' (parakalesai) the man so he is not swallowed up by excessive 'grief' (lype), then to 'ratify' (kyrosai, a completed past action in infinitive form of kyroo) their 'love' (agape) toward him. Galatians 6:1 commands 'restore, mend, set in order' (katartizete, an ongoing, simple present-tense command of katartizo, with the Liddell-Scott-Jones lexicon glossing it 'adjust, put in order, restore'), and Luke 17:3-4 makes 'if he repents, forgive him' (ean metanose, aphes auto) the rule, with 'forgive' (aphiemi) in both a completed past action command form and a future form. The verb 'ratify' (kyroo) occurs only twice in the whole Bible (here and Galatians 3:15, of a ratified covenant), and in both it means to make formally valid, so reaffirmed love is grammatically an official corporate act, not just a mood. The only over-specified element is the adverb 'publicly,' which the corporate agents imply but no anchor word actually states.

scripture.reasoning: The 'penalty' (epitimia, a noun in the subject form, feminine singular) is called 'sufficient' (ikanon) and is imposed 'by the majority' (hypo ton pleionon). The corporate agent and the note that the censure has done enough establish that discipline has a stopping point and a turning point toward restoration, not perpetual exclusion. 'This such one' (toioutos, in the to-or-for form, masculine singular) marks the same individual who is the object of forgiveness in verse 7.

The completed-past-action infinitives 'to forgive, graciously grant' (charisasthai, a completed past action infinitive) and 'to comfort' (parakalesai, a completed past action infinitive) name the positive duty after censure, lest the offender be 'swallowed up' (katapothe, a completed past passive subjunctive, third person singular) by excessive 'grief' (lype). 'Charizomai,' which the Liddell-Scott-Jones lexicon glosses 'to give grace,' carries free gracious release rather than mere acquittal, and it governs the offender as object.

Paul 'urges' (parakalo, an ongoing simple statement of fact, present tense, first person singular) the assembly to 'ratify' (kyrosai, a completed past action infinitive of kyroo) their 'love' (agape) 'toward him' (eis auton). 'Ratify' (kyroo) means to confirm or ratify (per the Liddell-Scott-Jones lexicon); its only other use in the whole Bible, Galatians 3:15, is 'a ratified covenant' (kekyromene diatheke), so the sense is a formal, performative validation. Pairing it with 'love' (agape) makes reaffirmed love an official, deliberate corporate act, the heart of the proposition.

Paul ties his own forgiveness to theirs ('but to whom you forgive,' ho de charizesthe, an ongoing simple statement of fact in present tense, second person plural, 'I also,' kago) and uses 'I have forgiven' (kecharismai, a completed action whose result still stands, first person singular). He locates it 'in the presence, or person, of Christ' (en prosopo Christou). Forgiveness of the disciplined is framed as reciprocal, settled, and done before Christ, grounding the corporate act in Christology (in the person and work of Christ).

The ongoing-present active command 'restore, mend, set right' (katartizete, an ongoing simple present-tense command, second person plural) tells the 'spiritual ones' (hoi pneumatikoi) to restore the one 'overtaken, caught' (prolemphthe, a completed past passive subjunctive, third person singular) in a trespass, 'in a spirit of gentleness' (en pneumati praytetos). 'Restore' (katartizo), which the Liddell-Scott-Jones lexicon glosses 'adjust, put in order, restore,' is used elsewhere of mending nets (Matthew 4:21) and of completing or perfecting (1 Thessalonians 3:10), so the force is reintegration, not punishment.

The 'if-then' clause 'if he repents, forgive him' (ean metanose, aphes auto) sets credible 'repentance' (metanoeo, a completed past action subjunctive, third person singular) as the trigger and 'forgiveness' (aphiemi, here 'forgive,' aphes, a completed past action command, second person singular) as the required response. 'Rebuke' (epitimeson, a completed past action command, second person singular) precedes, so the sequence rebuke then repentance then forgiveness mirrors discipline then restoration.

'Seven times' (heptakis) repentance in a day still obligates 'you shall forgive him' (apheseis auto, a future indicative form, second person singular). The future indicative (a simple statement about the future) functions as a command, and the repeated number underscores that repentance, however often renewed, is always met with forgiveness, leaving no room in the wording for withholding restoration from the credibly repentant.

The clause 'if anyone wanders from the truth and someone turns him back' (ean tis planethe apo tes aletheias kai epistrepse tis auton) presents the wanderer being 'turned back' (epistrepho, a completed past action subjunctive, third person singular) by a member of the community. The vocabulary frames restoration of a straying believer as a positive communal labor.

'The one who turns back' (ho epistrepsas, a completed past action participle, in the subject form, masculine singular) a sinner from the error of his way 'will save a soul from death' (sosei psychen ek thanatou, a future form, third person singular) and 'will cover a multitude of sins' (kalypsei plethos hamartion). The outcome language frames bringing the erring one back as life-giving covering, the goal of restoration.

Even toward the disciplined, 'do not regard him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother' (kai me hos echthron hegeisthe, alla noutheteite hos adelphon). The ongoing-present command 'admonish' (noutheteite) and the explicit 'as a brother' (hos adelphon) show that discipline does not strip brother status, so the relationship is preserved for restoration. OpenBible (the cross-reference dataset) links this verse to Galatians 6:1 at high vote, confirming the restorative trajectory (direction) of correction.

The Old Testament root of the rebuke-then-love pattern: 'do not hate your brother in your heart' (lo tisna et achikha), 'you shall surely rebuke your fellow' (hokeach tokiach et amitekha, from yakach, 'rebuke'). The infinitive-absolute plus finite verb construction (a Hebrew way of doubling a verb to intensify it), 'hokeach tokiach,' intensifies the duty to rebuke, set within the command not to hate, so corrective confrontation is itself an act of covenant love aimed at the brother, not his rejection. Luke 17:3 echoes this verse.

complicating_texts.resolution: First Corinthians 5:5 hands the offender over to Satan 'for destruction of the flesh' (eis olethron tes sarkos), which could read as terminal exclusion. But the purpose clause 'that the spirit may be saved' (hina to pneuma sothe, with sothe being a completed past passive subjunctive, third person singular) shows discipline is remedial (aimed at healing) and aimed at recovery, and 2 Corinthians 2 uses the same 'this such one' (toioutos) vocabulary reaching restoration. The complicating text reinforces the restorative goal rather than barring it.

Hebrews 6:4-6 says it is impossible to renew certain fallen ones 'to repentance' (eis metanoian). But the ongoing-present-tense participles 're-crucifying' (anastaurountas, a present participle, plural form) and 'holding up to contempt' (paradeigmatizontas) mark ongoing, persistent rejection with no repentance, whereas the proposition is conditioned on credible 'repentance' (metanoia). The two cases do not overlap, so this text does not contradict restoration of the repentant.

variant_units_examined.note: Witnesses differ on whether 'against you' (eis se) stands and on word order around 'seven times' (heptakis). The presence or absence of 'against you' (eis se) does not alter the forgiveness obligation tied to repentance, so the verdict is unaffected.

The opening verb varies between third singular 'let him know' (ginosketo) and second plural 'you know' (ginoskete), and the placement of 'his' (autou) varies. Neither changes the sense that turning a sinner back saves and covers, so restoration force is stable.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: The commands and infinitives 'to forgive' (charisasthai), 'to comfort' (parakalesai), 'to ratify' (kyrosai), 'restore' (katartizete), and 'forgive' (aphes), read in their immediate clauses, command forgiveness and reaffirmed love toward the repentant, directly supporting the proposition.

Reading the corporate agents ('by the majority,' hypo ton pleionon in 2 Corinthians 2:6, and the plural addressees of 'ratify' (kyrosai) and 'restore' (katartizete)) as the gathered assembly, the data shows restoration as a communal act of receiving the member back, with 2 Thessalonians 3:15 keeping the disciplined one classed 'as a brother' (hos adelphon).

A reader emphasizing the discipline texts (1 Corinthians 5, the rebuke in Luke 17:3, the handing over) could foreground confrontation, yet the very vocabulary they rely on is conditioned: 'penalty' (epitimia) is 'sufficient' (ikanon, with a stopping point), 1 Corinthians 5:5 carries 'that the spirit may be saved' (hina to pneuma sothe), and Luke 17:3 pairs 'rebuke' (epitimeson) with 'if he repents, forgive' (ean metanose, aphes). On the lexical data this lens still lands on restoration once repentance is credible; it differs only on the threshold and process, not the duty.

hermeneutics.notes: Verdict rests on the analogy of scripture (the principle that clearer passages interpret less clear ones, and that the whole Bible agrees with itself): distinct authors (Paul, Luke, James) plus the Leviticus 19 root converge on the same restorative duty toward the repentant, with no contrary lexical witness once unrepentant-apostasy (persistent, willful turning away from the faith) texts are scoped out by their own grammar.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: When a disciplined member shows credible repentance, how does the assembly respond regarding forgiveness, reaffirmation of love, and the manner (private or public) of receiving them back?
stem_audit.notes: The adverb 'publicly' is an inference, not a lexical datum (a fact drawn straight from the wording itself). The texts establish corporate agency (the majority imposed the penalty; the assembly is urged to ratify love) but no anchor verse contains a term meaning 'openly' or 'before all.' The verdict is derived on the original stem; the forgiving and reaffirming-love core is strongly attested, while the 'publicly' element is supported only by the corporate verbs ('ratify,' kyrosai, addressed to the assembly, 'restore,' katartizete, to the spiritual ones) and not by an explicit lexeme (a single word carrying that meaning). This partial gap is named as over-specification; it does not lower confidence on the substantive claim.

lay_summary: The passages behind this question point the same direction in their original wording. In Second Corinthians 2 Paul says the penalty (epitimia) the assembly imposed, a censure by the majority, has been enough (sufficient, ikanon), and now the church should do something positive. He uses charizomai, a verb of gracious forgiving, and parakaleo, to comfort, so the disciplined man is not swallowed up by too much sorrow (lype). He then asks them to formally confirm or ratify (kyrosai, a completed past action infinitive form of kyroo) their love (agape) for him. The verb kyroo is a formal word meaning to ratify or confirm, and it appears only twice in the whole New Testament, here and in Galatians 3 of a legally ratified covenant. Because both uses agree, the sense is not in doubt: reaffirming love is treated as a deliberate, official corporate act, not a vague feeling. Galatians 6:1 uses katartizo (its ordinary meaning is to mend, set in order, restore, the same word for repairing nets) and commands the spiritually mature to restore (katartizete, an ongoing simple present-tense command) someone caught in a fault, gently. Luke 17:3-4 makes the logic plain: if he repents (metanoeo, turns around in mind), forgive (aphiemi) him, even seven times (heptakis) in a day. James 5 praises the one who turns back (epistrepho) a wandering believer, saying it saves a soul from death and covers many sins, and Second Thessalonians 3:15 says even the disciplined person is to be treated not as an enemy but admonished as a brother (adelphos). The root reaches back to Leviticus 19, where rebuking (yakach) a fellow Israelite is set inside the command not to hate him. Across this whole chain the vocabulary of forgiving, restoring, turning back, and confirming love consistently follows genuine repentance, and the two texts that might seem to block restoration, the handing over in First Corinthians 5 and the no-renewal warning in Hebrews 6, actually aim at recovery or describe ongoing unrepentant turning-away. The one element the wording does not directly state is the adverb publicly. The texts show the whole assembly acting together, which implies an open reception, but no single Greek word means 'in public' or 'before all.' So the core claim, forgive and reaffirm love toward the credibly repentant, is strongly and broadly attested, while the specifically public manner is implied by corporate action rather than stated outright. That small gap, not any contrary teaching, is the only place the words leave room.
